disease.name: Sinusitis
disease.scientific_name: Rhinosinusitis / Acute Bacterial Rhinosinusitis (ABRS) / Chronic Rhinosinusitis (CRS) / Viral Rhinosinusitis / Invasive Fungal Rhinosinusitis

disease.category: Otorhinolaryngology (ENT) / Respiratory Medicine / Allergy / Infectious Disease

overview.description: Rhinosinusitis — commonly called sinusitis — is inflammation of the mucous membranes lining the paranasal sinuses (the air-filled cavities within the facial bones: maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses) and their continuity with the nasal mucosa. The term 'rhinosinusitis' is now preferred over 'sinusitis' because sinusitis almost never occurs without concurrent nasal mucosal inflammation (rhinitis) — the nasal cavity and sinuses share a continuous mucosal lining, and inflammation invariably affects both simultaneously. Sinusitis is one of the most prevalent conditions encountered in primary care globally — affecting 10-15% of the general population, accounting for approximately 40 million doctor consultations annually in the USA alone, and representing one of the most common conditions for which antibiotics are prescribed (though the vast majority of cases are viral and do not require antibiotics). The disease exists along a clinical spectrum: at one end, the common cold (acute viral rhinosinusitis) — an almost universal human experience, self-limiting within 7-10 days; in the middle, acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS) — affecting only 0.5-2% of viral rhinosinusitis episodes, requiring antibiotic therapy; and at the other extreme, invasive fungal rhinosinusitis — a rapidly progressive, potentially fatal condition in immunocompromised individuals (dramatically highlighted by the COVID-19-associated mucormycosis epidemic in India in 2021 — 'black fungus'). Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) — defined as inflammation persisting beyond 12 weeks — is a major cause of impaired quality of life, affecting productivity, sleep, and cognitive function. India faces unique sinusitis challenges: extremely high urban air pollution (Delhi AQI regularly exceeds 400-500 — 'hazardous' category, causing mucociliary dysfunction and mucosal inflammation); perennial allergic rhinitis from dust mite, cockroach, mould, and pollen allergens driving CRS; and the catastrophic mucormycosis outbreak during the COVID-19 second wave (2021) which caused over 45,000 cases and significant mortality.
overview.affected_organ: Paranasal sinuses (maxillary — most commonly affected; ethmoid; frontal; sphenoid), nasal cavity, nasal mucosa, osteomeatal complex (the key drainage pathway); potential spread to orbit, anterior skull base, intracranial cavity

sinus_anatomy.maxillary_sinuses: Largest sinuses; located in the cheekbones bilaterally; drain via ostia into the middle meatus; most commonly affected in sinusitis; symptoms: cheek pain and pressure; dental pain (upper molar roots in close proximity); purulent nasal discharge
sinus_anatomy.ethmoid_sinuses: Multiple small air cells between the eyes (medial orbital wall); divided into anterior (drain to middle meatus) and posterior (drain to superior meatus); pain between and behind the eyes; commonly affected in children (largest sinuses relatively in children); the key passage for spread of infection to orbit
sinus_anatomy.frontal_sinuses: Located in the forehead above the eyebrows; absent at birth, develop through childhood; drain via frontal recess into middle meatus; frontal sinusitis causes severe forehead pain, worse on leaning forward; most dangerous sinus for intracranial complications (proximity to anterior cranial fossa)
sinus_anatomy.sphenoid_sinuses: Deepest sinuses, located at the centre of the skull base; drain into sphenoethmoidal recess; sphenoid sinusitis causes poorly localised deep 'vertex' headache, retro-orbital pain; dangerous location — adjacent to optic nerve, cavernous sinus, pituitary gland, and internal carotid artery

overview.prevalence: Global: 10-15% of adults affected by acute sinusitis annually; 5-12% have chronic rhinosinusitis; India: estimated 30-40 million sinusitis cases annually; very high prevalence of allergic rhinitis (perennial — 20-30% of urban Indians) driving CRS; urban-rural divide — urban Indians at much higher risk from air pollution exposure; COVID-19-associated mucormycosis 2021 — India recorded 45,000+ cases (90% of world's total) making mucormycosis a major public health crisis
overview.age_group: All ages; acute viral rhinosinusitis most frequent in young children (6-8 upper respiratory infections per year); allergic rhinosinusitis peaks in teens and young adults; CRS with nasal polyps peaks in adults 30-60 years (predominantly male); invasive fungal sinusitis in immunocompromised adults
overview.is_contagious_note: Viral rhinosinusitis (the common cold) is highly contagious — spread by respiratory droplets and contact with contaminated surfaces; bacterial sinusitis itself is not directly contagious but the viral triggers are
overview.is_curable_note: Acute viral sinusitis resolves spontaneously; acute bacterial sinusitis cured with antibiotics; chronic rhinosinusitis is managed rather than cured — symptoms controlled with INCS, saline irrigation, and/or surgery; nasal polyps recur in 40-60% after surgery
overview.key_fact: Antibiotics are overprescribed for sinusitis in India — approximately 85-90% of sinusitis cases are caused by viruses against which antibiotics have zero effect. The cardinal rule: GREEN or CLEAR nasal discharge does NOT mean bacterial infection — colour is determined by neutrophil breakdown, not bacteria. Antibiotics for sinusitis should be reserved for the 0.5-2% of cases with confirmed bacterial superinfection — characterised by worsening after initial improvement (double worsening), fever >38.5°C, severe unilateral facial pain, or symptoms persisting beyond 10 days without improvement.

types.name: Acute Viral Rhinosinusitis (AVRS) — The Common Cold
types.description: By far the most common form — accounting for 98-99% of all acute rhinosinusitis presentations. Caused by respiratory viruses that infect the nasal and sinus mucosa, causing mucosal oedema, increased mucus secretion, and temporary obstruction of sinus ostia (the natural drainage openings). AVRS is self-limiting — the immune system clears the viral infection within 7-10 days without any specific treatment. The normal progression: watery clear discharge → thicker, cloudy, or yellow-green discharge over days 3-5 (this colour change is NORMAL viral evolution — does NOT indicate bacterial superinfection).
types.causative_viruses: Rhinovirus (most common — 50% of adult colds; >100 serotypes); Coronavirus (including SARS-CoV-2); Adenovirus; Influenza A and B; Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV — particularly in children); Parainfluenza virus; Metapneumovirus
types.clinical_course: Incubation 1-3 days; Peak symptoms days 2-4; Resolution within 7-10 days; Symptoms lasting >10 days without improvement raise suspicion of bacterial superinfection or allergic component
types.management: SYMPTOMATIC ONLY — NO ANTIBIOTICS: adequate hydration; paracetamol for fever and headache; saline nasal irrigation (nasal douching — highly effective); short-term topical decongestant (oxymetazoline maximum 3-5 days — prevents rebound congestion); steam inhalation; honey (for cough in children over 1 year — has evidence of equivalent efficacy to dextromethorphan); rest
types.india_note: The 'common cold' leads to vast inappropriate antibiotic prescribing in India — a major driver of antimicrobial resistance; patient and public education that colds are viral and antibiotics are useless is urgently needed

types.name: Acute Bacterial Rhinosinusitis (ABRS)
types.description: Bacterial superinfection complicating viral rhinosinusitis — occurring in only 0.5-2% of viral upper respiratory infections. ABRS results when viral mucosal oedema obstructs sinus ostia → impaired mucociliary clearance → retained secretions → bacterial proliferation in the warm, moist, anaerobic sinus environment. Distinguishing ABRS from prolonged viral rhinosinusitis is the most important clinical challenge — overprescription of antibiotics for viral sinusitis is rampant.
types.causative_bacteria: Streptococcus pneumoniae (30-35% — most common; may cause severe complications); Haemophilus influenzae (25-30% — non-typeable; often beta-lactamase producing in India); Moraxella catarrhalis (10-15% — very high spontaneous resolution rate ~75%); Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA); Mixed anaerobes (particularly in odontogenic sinusitis); Pseudomonas aeruginosa (in immunocompromised, CF, nosocomial)

diagnostic_criteria_AVRS_vs_ABRS.three_clinical_criteria: ABRS is clinically diagnosed when ONE of the following three criteria is met:
diagnostic_criteria_AVRS_vs_ABRS.criteria_1: PERSISTENT SYMPTOMS beyond 10 days without improvement (the most common presentation of ABRS) — a cold that simply hasn't got better at all by day 10 suggests bacterial superinfection
diagnostic_criteria_AVRS_vs_ABRS.criteria_2: SEVERE SYMPTOMS or SIGNS from the outset — fever ≥39°C AND purulent (thick yellow-green) nasal discharge AND facial pain/pressure — all three simultaneously — for at least 3-4 consecutive days
diagnostic_criteria_AVRS_vs_ABRS.criteria_3: 'DOUBLE WORSENING' — symptoms initially improving (typical viral cold pattern) but then WORSENING again after initial improvement (worsening of fever, pain, discharge after day 5-7 of a cold) — the most specific clinical indicator of bacterial superinfection

types.management: Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin) is first-line in India: 625 mg (500+125) three times daily × 5-7 days; or 1g (875+125) twice daily × 5-7 days; intranasal corticosteroid (INCS) adjunct; saline irrigation; decongestant for first 3-5 days only

types.name: Chronic Rhinosinusitis Without Nasal Polyps (CRSsNP)
types.description: Chronic rhinosinusitis is defined as inflammation of the sinonasal mucosa persisting for at least 12 weeks with objective evidence of disease (by endoscopy or CT scan) despite adequate medical treatment. CRS without nasal polyps (CRSsNP) involves diffuse mucosal thickening and fibrosis without the formation of polypoid (grape-like) tissue. The dominant feature is mucosal thickening, not polyps. CRSsNP is associated with neutrophilic (Th1-mediated) inflammation — distinct from the eosinophilic (Th2-mediated) inflammation of CRSwNP.
types.pathophysiology: Recurrent acute infections; persistent bacterial biofilm formation (particularly Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas); mucociliary dysfunction (impaired mucosal 'escalator' clearing bacteria and particles); anatomical factors (deviated nasal septum — DNS, concha bullosa, agger nasi cells obstructing ostiomeatal complex); environmental factors (pollution, allergens, cigarette smoke); immune dysfunction
types.clinical_features: Two or more of: nasal congestion/blockage; mucopurulent nasal discharge (anterior or posterior drip); facial pain/pressure; reduction or loss of smell (hyposmia/anosmia); PLUS objective confirmation by nasal endoscopy (mucopus in middle meatus) or CT scan (mucosal thickening ≥3-4 mm)
types.india_specific: CRSsNP is disproportionately common in Indian cities due to chronic air pollution exposure — particulate matter (PM2.5, PM10) directly damages mucosal cilia and triggers chronic mucosal inflammation; occupational exposures (chemical fumes, wood dust, grain dust); biomass fuel combustion (chulha — indoor pollution)
types.management: Intranasal corticosteroids (INCS — mometasone, fluticasone, budesonide) are the cornerstone of treatment; nasal saline irrigation twice daily; treat underlying allergic rhinitis; short antibiotic courses for bacterial exacerbations; functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) if medical treatment fails after 3-6 months

types.name: Chronic Rhinosinusitis With Nasal Polyps (CRSwNP)
types.description: The second major CRS phenotype — characterised by the presence of bilateral nasal polyps (grape-like, semi-transparent, non-tender, smooth mucosal overgrowths) arising primarily from the ethmoid sinuses and extending into the nasal cavity. CRSwNP involves eosinophilic (Th2-mediated, Type 2) inflammation with dramatically elevated IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 cytokines and markedly raised local IgE. This Th2 endotype is important because it defines the target for biologic therapies (dupilumab — anti-IL-4Rα) and explains the association with asthma and aspirin sensitivity.
associated_conditions: Asthma — present in 20-40% of CRSwNP patients; the 'united airway disease' concept: upper and lower airway inflammation are biologically linked via shared Th2/eosinophilic inflammation; sinusitis and asthma exacerbate each other

Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD / Samter's Triad): nasal polyps + asthma + aspirin sensitivity; aspirin and NSAIDs trigger severe bronchoconstriction and nasal reaction; affects 10-15% of CRSwNP patients; aspirin desensitisation therapy may be beneficial
Allergic Rhinitis — common comorbidity; IgE-mediated mucosal inflammation promotes polyp formation
Cystic fibrosis — bilateral polyps in children (always test sweat chloride in young CRSwNP patients)
Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) — mucociliary dysfunction; Kartagener syndrome (situs inversus + bronchiectasis + sinusitis)
types.clinical_features: Severe nasal obstruction (often bilateral and complete); profound loss of smell (anosmia — most distressing symptom; sometimes permanent); posterior nasal drip; snoring; mouth breathing; muffled voice; pale smooth bilateral nasal polyps visible on anterior rhinoscopy
types.management: INCS (high-dose topical); systemic corticosteroids for acute exacerbations; dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα biologic — dramatically effective for severe CRSwNP; reduces polyp size and exacerbations; currently very expensive in India); FESS with polypectomy; aspirin desensitisation for AERD; mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) for eosinophilic CRSwNP with asthma
types.recurrence: Nasal polyp recurrence rate after FESS: 40-60% within 5 years; higher in AERD and severe eosinophilia; biologic therapy significantly reduces recurrence rates

types.name: Invasive Fungal Rhinosinusitis (IFS) — Medical Emergency
types.description: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening fungal infection of the sinonasal tissues with angio-invasion (blood vessel invasion by fungal hyphae) causing tissue ischaemia and necrosis — predominantly affecting immunocompromised individuals. Invasive fungal sinusitis has a mortality rate of 30-80% despite maximal treatment. The COVID-19 pandemic and its treatment (particularly high-dose corticosteroid use in diabetic or immune-compromised patients) triggered a catastrophic mucormycosis epidemic in India in 2021 — the country accounted for >90% of all global COVID-19-associated mucormycosis (CAM) cases.

subtypes.name: Acute Invasive Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AIFRS)
subtypes.description: Fulminant, rapidly progressive; mortality 50-80%; organisms: Mucorales (mucormycosis — predominantly Rhizopus, Mucor, Cunninghamella); Aspergillus fumigatus (less common but important); Fusarium; characteristic: black necrotic tissue (eschars — black because of angioinvasion causing ischaemic necrosis); spreads rapidly to orbit (orbital apex syndrome) and brain (cerebral involvement = 100% fatal without aggressive surgery)
subtypes.risk_factors: Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (DKA — most important risk factor in India; iron released from low pH environment facilitates Mucorales growth); high-dose corticosteroid therapy; neutropenia (chemotherapy, haematological malignancy, aplastic anaemia); HIV/AIDS with CD4 <100; transplantation; deferoxamine therapy (iron chelator — paradoxically provides iron substrate for Mucorales); COVID-19 + diabetes + corticosteroids (the COVID-19-associated mucormycosis triad)

subtypes.name: Chronic Invasive Fungal Rhinosinusitis
subtypes.description: Slowly progressive over months (vs weeks for acute form); organisms: Aspergillus most common; affects immunocompetent but debilitated patients; less fulminant but destructive; better prognosis than acute form

subtypes.name: Granulomatous Invasive Fungal Rhinosinusitis
subtypes.description: Rare; predominantly in Sudan and India; Aspergillus flavus; immunocompetent patients; forms granulomata; presents with proptosis (orbital extension); treatment: surgery + itraconazole

subtypes.name: Non-Invasive Fungal Sinusitis
subtypes.description: Two forms: (1) Fungal Ball (Mycetoma): dense collection of fungal hyphae in a sinus (usually maxillary) without mucosal invasion; immunocompetent; no antifungal treatment needed — surgery alone curative; (2) Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AFRS): Th2 immune reaction to fungal allergens (predominantly dematiaceous/darkly pigmented fungi: Bipolaris, Curvularia, Alternaria) producing eosinophilic mucin and tissue eosinophilia without tissue invasion; associated with nasal polyps; management: FESS + INCS + anti-IgE therapy

types.warning_signs_invasive: BLACK ESCHAR (necrotic tissue) inside nose or on palate — EMERGENCY; unilateral proptosis (orbital extension); visual loss; facial numbness or palsy; new cranial nerve deficits in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient with sinus symptoms = EMERGENCY CT SCAN AND URGENT ENT REFERRAL

covid_mucormycosis_india_2021.description: India's COVID-19 second wave (April-June 2021) was complicated by a massive mucormycosis outbreak — 45,000+ cases vs 200-300 cases per year normally; case fatality rate 50-60% despite treatment; 'black fungus' became a notifiable disease in India (May 2021)
covid_mucormycosis_india_2021.risk_triad: COVID-19 infection (impairs innate immunity) + Corticosteroids (dexamethasone given to most hospitalised patients — further immunosuppression; hyperglycaemia) + Diabetes mellitus (present in 60-70% of CAM patients; DKA environment releases free iron; hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function)
covid_mucormycosis_india_2021.treatment_cam: IV amphotericin B (liposomal formulation preferred — less nephrotoxic); surgical debridement (aggressive — extensive resection of all necrotic tissue including orbital exenteration if needed); control diabetes (tight glycaemic control); reduce/stop corticosteroids; isavuconazole or posaconazole as step-down oral therapy

types.name: Odontogenic Sinusitis
types.description: Sinusitis originating from dental pathology — specifically from the upper posterior teeth (upper premolars and molars) whose roots are in close proximity to or project into the floor of the maxillary sinus. A significantly underdiagnosed cause of chronic unilateral sinusitis (15-20% of chronic maxillary sinusitis). Important to distinguish from primary rhinosinusitis because: (1) treatment requires addressing the dental source; (2) microbiology is different (mixed anaerobes — foul smell distinctive); (3) unilateral maxillary sinusitis not responding to standard treatment should always raise suspicion.
types.dental_causes: Periapical abscess from upper molar/premolar; failed root canal treatment; dental implants breaching sinus floor; tooth extraction creating oro-antral fistula; periodontal disease with periapical pathology
types.clinical_features: Unilateral maxillary sinusitis (bilateral rare); foul-smelling (fetid) nasal discharge (anaerobic infection characteristic); dental pain or history of recent dental procedure; failure to respond to standard antibiotics; CT scan showing unilateral maxillary disease with dental pathology (periapical abscess, retained root fragment, implant breach)
types.management: Treat dental source (tooth extraction, root canal revision, implant removal); FESS maxillary antrostomy for drainage; antibiotics targeting anaerobes (co-amoxiclav or metronidazole + amoxicillin)

types.name: Allergic Rhinosinusitis
types.description: Rhinosinusitis driven by IgE-mediated (Type I hypersensitivity) reaction to inhaled allergens — causing bilateral mucosal inflammation that predisposes to CRS by impairing mucociliary clearance, promoting mucosal oedema at ostia, and creating an eosinophilic inflammatory environment. Allergic rhinitis is the single most important predisposing condition for recurrent and chronic sinusitis. India has very high perennial allergic rhinitis prevalence (20-30% in urban adults) from: house dust mites (Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus, D. farinae — the dominant allergen in tropical climates); cockroach allergen (Blatella germanica — very common in Indian households); moulds (Aspergillus, Alternaria — related to monsoon humidity and biomass fuel exposure); pollen (seasonal — trees in spring, grasses in early summer); pet dander (less common).
types.management: Allergen avoidance; antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine); INCS; allergen immunotherapy (subcutaneous SCIT or sublingual SLIT — disease-modifying treatment for allergic rhinitis; reduces nasal polyp risk; available at allergy centres in India — AIIMS, PGI, major private hospitals); anti-IgE (omalizumab — for severe allergic rhinosinusitis with asthma)

severity_levels.name: Mild — Viral Rhinosinusitis or Mild ABRS
severity_levels.description: Self-limiting viral sinusitis or mild bacterial sinusitis with minor impact on daily function.
severity_levels.criteria: Symptoms <10 days (viral) or <7 days bacterial criteria; no fever or low-grade fever <38°C; mild-moderate nasal obstruction and discharge; facial discomfort rather than severe pain; able to work and perform daily activities; no alarm features
severity_levels.functional_impact: Minor inconvenience; able to continue most daily activities; sleep mildly disturbed
severity_levels.management: Home management; saline nasal irrigation (twice daily); paracetamol for discomfort; short-term oxymetazoline (maximum 3-5 days); steam inhalation; adequate hydration; review if not improving in 10 days (viral) or 48-72 hours without improvement on antibiotics (ABRS)
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Symptoms worsening after initial improvement (double worsening); fever developing >38.5°C; severe facial pain; symptoms persisting >10 days

severity_levels.name: Moderate — Persistent ABRS or CRS Exacerbation
severity_levels.description: Bacterial sinusitis meeting criteria for antibiotic therapy, or CRS with significant impact on quality of life.
severity_levels.criteria: Symptoms >10 days without improvement; OR double worsening; OR severe symptoms with fever ≥38.5°C + facial pain + purulent discharge for ≥3 days; CRS with visual analogue scale (VAS) total symptom score ≥5/10; significant impairment of work/school performance; sleep disturbance
severity_levels.functional_impact: Significantly reduces quality of life; missed work; moderate pain; impaired smell affecting food enjoyment
severity_levels.management: GP assessment; antibiotic if ABRS criteria met (co-amoxiclav 625 mg TDS × 5-7 days); INCS adjunct; saline irrigation; consider CT if diagnosis uncertain; ENT referral if recurrent (≥3 episodes per year) or CRS not responding to 3 months INCS

severity_levels.name: Severe — Complicated Sinusitis or Refractory CRS
severity_levels.description: Sinusitis causing significant morbidity from orbital involvement, severe intracranial symptoms, or refractory CRS significantly impairing quality of life.
severity_levels.criteria: Periorbital oedema or erythema; any diplopia, visual change, or proptosis; severe unilateral facial pain; neurological symptoms (severe headache, altered consciousness, meningism); CRS VAS >7/10 with nasal polyps; bilateral complete nasal obstruction; severe anosmia affecting nutrition and quality of life
severity_levels.functional_impact: Significantly impairs daily life; orbital symptoms require emergency ENT referral; refractory CRS may require surgery
severity_levels.management: URGENT ENT assessment (same day for orbital symptoms); CT sinuses and orbits; IV antibiotics for orbital cellulitis; FESS planning for refractory CRS; biologic therapy assessment for severe CRSwNP

severity_levels.name: Critical — Intracranial Complications or Invasive Fungal Sinusitis
severity_levels.description: Life-threatening complications from intracranial spread or rapidly progressive invasive fungal sinusitis requiring emergency intervention.
severity_levels.criteria: Meningism (neck stiffness + photophobia + headache); altered consciousness or confusion; seizures; cavernous sinus thrombosis signs (bilateral proptosis, chemosis, cranial nerve III/IV/VI palsies); black necrotic tissue in nasal cavity or palate (invasive fungal sinusitis); complete visual loss; Pott's puffy tumour (forehead swelling + frontal sinusitis); septicaemia
severity_levels.management: EMERGENCY: call 102/112; neurosurgery + ENT joint management; brain MRI/CT with contrast; IV antibiotics or antifungals; surgical drainage and debridement; ICU monitoring; liposomal amphotericin B for mucormycosis
severity_levels.mortality: Cavernous sinus thrombosis: 20-30% even with treatment; Invasive mucormycosis with cerebral involvement: >80% mortality

causative_agents_overview.viral: 98% of acute rhinosinusitis — rhinovirus, coronavirus, adenovirus, influenza, RSV, parainfluenza
causative_agents_overview.bacterial: 0.5-2% of acute rhinosinusitis — Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis
causative_agents_overview.fungal: Mucorales (mucormycosis), Aspergillus, Bipolaris, Curvularia — invasive in immunocompromised; non-invasive (fungal ball, AFRS) in immunocompetent
causative_agents_overview.allergic: IgE-mediated eosinophilic inflammation from allergens — dust mites, cockroach, moulds, pollen
causative_agents_overview.anatomical: Deviated nasal septum (DNS), nasal polyps, concha bullosa, hypertrophied turbinates — obstructing ostia

risk_factors: Viral upper respiratory infection — by far the most important trigger for acute bacterial sinusitis (viral mucosal oedema obstructs ostia → bacterial superinfection)

Allergic rhinitis — chronic mucosal inflammation impairs mucociliary clearance; eosinophilic inflammation promotes polyp formation and ostial obstruction; the single most important comorbidity for recurrent and chronic sinusitis

Air pollution — India-specific: chronic exposure to PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen dioxide, ozone, and indoor smoke (biomass fuel — chulha burning wood, dung, and crop waste); directly damages sinonasal mucociliary apparatus; promotes chronic inflammation; major driver of CRS prevalence in Indian cities; Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata regularly among world's most polluted cities
Cigarette smoking and passive smoke — impairs mucociliary function (cilia become immotile); increases mucus viscosity; damages respiratory epithelium; increases CRS risk 2-3×

Deviated Nasal Septum (DNS) — very prevalent in India (30-40% of adults); DNS narrows the middle meatus and impairs sinus drainage; contributes to recurrent sinusitis particularly maxillary and ethmoid
Swimming and diving — water forced into sinuses; chlorinated water irritates mucosa; swimmer's sinusitis (P. aeruginosa prominent)
Dental disease — particularly upper molar and premolar periapical abscesses (odontogenic sinusitis); very common in India where dental care access is limited

Immune deficiency — HIV/AIDS; primary immunodeficiencies (IgA deficiency, CVID, CGD); chemotherapy; organ transplantation; long-term corticosteroids; recurrent sinusitis is a cardinal feature of common variable immunodeficiency (CVID)
Diabetes mellitus — impairs neutrophil function; promotes fungal growth (Mucorales thrive in high-glucose, low-pH environments); particularly dangerous combination with DKA for mucormycosis risk
Nasal foreign bodies — especially in children (unilateral foul-smelling discharge in a child = nasal foreign body until proven otherwise)

Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) — reflux of acid/pepsin into the nasopharynx (laryngopharyngeal reflux — LPR) causes posterior pharyngeal and sinonasal mucosal inflammation; important but controversial contributor to CRS
Cystic fibrosis and primary ciliary dyskinesia — structural mucociliary dysfunction causing universal CRS and nasal polyps from childhood

Anatomical variants — concha bullosa (pneumatised middle turbinate); Haller cells (infraorbital ethmoid cells narrowing sinus drainage); agger nasi cells; accessory maxillary ostia — all potentially impair normal sinus drainage
Workplace exposures — woodworking dust (maxillary adenocarcinoma and CRS); grain dust; chemical exposures; hairdresser chemicals
Psychological stress — impairs mucosal immune function; increases susceptibility to viral infections
Damp housing and mould exposure — particularly relevant in India during monsoon season; Aspergillus and other moulds trigger allergic fungal rhinosinusitis

symptoms.overview: Rhinosinusitis symptoms arise from three mechanisms: mucosal inflammation causing local pain and swelling; impaired drainage causing pressure accumulation within air-filled sinuses; and systemic effects of infection causing fever and malaise. Symptom pattern is diagnostically important — location of facial pain correlates with the sinus affected; bilateral symmetric symptoms suggest allergic or viral aetiology; unilateral symptoms (particularly unilateral foul-smelling discharge) suggest bacterial or odontogenic cause. The four CARDINAL SYMPTOMS of rhinosinusitis are: (1) nasal obstruction/congestion; (2) nasal discharge (anterior rhinorrhoea or posterior nasal drip); (3) facial pain or pressure; (4) reduction/loss of smell (hyposmia/anosmia). Diagnosis of CRS requires ≥2 of these symptoms for ≥12 weeks.

primary_symptoms.name: Nasal Congestion and Obstruction
primary_symptoms.description: Blockage of nasal airflow from mucosal oedema, increased secretions, and in CRSwNP from physical obstruction by polypoid tissue. Ranges from partial blockage (congestion) to complete bilateral obstruction. In CRSwNP: complete bilateral nasal obstruction is typical — patients describe 'breathing through two blocked pipes'; mouth breathing; snoring; sleep disruption. In acute sinusitis: obstruction is from mucosal swelling — usually unilateral or bilateral but variable. Nasal obstruction causes: inability to breathe through nose; hyponasality (muffled 'nasal' voice — 'nasal voice' of a cold — actually hyponasal when nose is blocked); difficulty sleeping; mouth breathing leading to dry mouth and sore throat.

primary_symptoms.name: Nasal Discharge (Rhinorrhoea)
primary_symptoms.description: Excessive nasal secretions — characteristically ANTERIOR (dripping from the front of the nose — 'runny nose') in viral rhinitis; and POSTERIOR (post-nasal drip — mucus draining into the throat from the back of the nose) in sinusitis and CRS. CHARACTER OF DISCHARGE: CLEAR/WATERY = viral rhinitis, allergic rhinitis, vasomotor rhinitis; YELLOW-GREEN (purulent) = bacterial sinusitis OR (importantly) NORMAL viral evolution at days 3-5 of a cold; FOUL-SMELLING = odontogenic sinusitis (anaerobic) or invasive fungal sinusitis; BLOODY = tumour, nasal polyp bleeding, severe inflammation, foreign body, or angiofibroma (young males). POST-NASAL DRIP: mucus draining down the posterior pharynx causing: chronic throat clearing; cough (especially nocturnal); hoarseness; sensation of something stuck in the throat.
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: YELLOW-GREEN discharge alone does NOT indicate bacterial infection — this is the most common misconception leading to inappropriate antibiotic prescribing; colour is from myeloperoxidase in neutrophils, not bacteria

primary_symptoms.name: Facial Pain, Pressure, and Headache
primary_symptoms.description: The sinus-specific pattern of pain is diagnostically useful: MAXILLARY SINUSITIS: cheek pain and pressure; malar (cheekbone) tenderness to palpation; toothache or dental sensitivity in upper teeth; pain worsens on leaning forward (fluid shifts toward blocked ostium); FRONTAL SINUSITIS: severe forehead pain above the eyebrows; worse in the morning (drainage impaired when lying flat); may be very severe and throbbing; ETHMOID SINUSITIS: pain between the eyes (medial canthal region); retro-orbital pressure; may radiate to the temples; SPHENOID SINUSITIS: 'vertex' headache (top of head); retro-orbital pain; deep facial pain poorly localised; 'worst headache of my life' can indicate cavernous sinus extension — EMERGENCY. HEADACHE PATTERN: sinusitis headache is NOT throbbing (migraine is); NOT worsened by bright light or noise (migraine features); IS worsened by bending forward, nose-blowing, or Valsalva.
primary_symptoms.note: Persistent very severe headache or headache with neurological features should raise concern for intracranial complications — urgent imaging

primary_symptoms.name: Loss of Smell — Hyposmia and Anosmia
primary_symptoms.description: Reduction (hyposmia) or complete loss (anosmia) of the sense of smell — one of the most distressing and quality-of-life-impairing symptoms of sinusitis, particularly CRS with nasal polyps. MECHANISMS: CONDUCTIVE anosmia — mucosal swelling or polyps physically blocking odorant molecules from reaching the olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity (the most common mechanism in sinusitis — potentially reversible with treatment); SENSORINEURAL anosmia — damage to olfactory receptor neurons from chronic inflammation (partially reversible); Loss of smell causes: inability to appreciate food flavours (most flavour is smell-dependent — taste detects only sweet/salty/sour/bitter/umami; the rest is retronasal olfaction); loss of safety warning from gas leaks or fire; loss of social confidence (cannot detect own body odour); depression and anxiety. COVID-19 anosmia: distinct from sinusitis anosmia — caused by direct viral damage to olfactory sustentacular cells without nasal obstruction; rapid onset; often no nasal congestion.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild (hyposmia) to Complete (anosmia in severe CRSwNP)

secondary_symptoms: Fever — low-grade (37.5-38.5°C) in ABRS; high fever (>38.5°C) is uncommon and may indicate complications; fever with sinusitis in immunocompromised = consider invasive fungal sinusitis
Halitosis (bad breath) — from purulent nasal discharge draining into oropharynx; anaerobic bacteria in sinuses produce volatile sulphur compounds; distinctive in odontogenic sinusitis

Facial swelling — periorbital oedema (around the eyes) is the most common sign of orbital extension from ethmoid sinusitis; forehead swelling (Pott's puffy tumour) from frontal sinusitis with osteomyelitis
Cough — particularly nocturnal; from postnasal drip irritating the larynx and trachea; very common in children with sinusitis (may be the presenting symptom)

Ear pressure or fullness — from Eustachian tube dysfunction (the Eustachian tube drains into the nasopharynx; swollen adenoids and posterior nasal oedema impair its function); 'blocked ears'; reduced hearing; otitis media in children
Sleep disturbance — nasal obstruction forces mouth breathing; interrupted sleep from pain and snoring; sleep deprivation worsens immunity and prolongs illness
Fatigue and malaise — from systemic inflammation, sleep disruption, reduced oxygenation from nasal obstruction; particularly pronounced in CRS
Snoring and sleep-disordered breathing — severe CRS with nasal polyps causes obstructive breathing during sleep; may contribute to obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA)
Throat irritation and soreness — from postnasal drip and mouth breathing causing pharyngeal dryness
Photophobia (light sensitivity) — in frontal or sphenoid sinusitis; raises concern for meningeal irritation if severe

sinus_specific_pain_locations.maxillary: Cheek, upper teeth, infraorbital region; worse on leaning forward
sinus_specific_pain_locations.frontal: Forehead; between and above the eyebrows; worse in morning
sinus_specific_pain_locations.ethmoid: Between and behind the eyes; medial canthal region; may cause orbital pain
sinus_specific_pain_locations.sphenoid: Vertex (top of head); retro-orbital; diffuse deep facial pain; may radiate to occiput (back of head)

alarm_signs_requiring_urgent_attention: Periorbital swelling, erythema, or oedema — orbital cellulitis from ethmoid sinusitis; URGENT SAME-DAY ENT assessment
Proptosis (bulging eye) — orbital abscess or cavernous sinus thrombosis; EMERGENCY
Diplopia (double vision) — orbital apex involvement; cranial nerve palsy; EMERGENCY
Visual loss or change — orbital complications threatening optic nerve; TIME-CRITICAL emergency
Severe headache with neck stiffness and photophobia — meningitis from sinus extension; EMERGENCY
Altered consciousness, confusion, or seizures — intracranial complication; EMERGENCY
Forehead swelling with frontal sinusitis — Pott's puffy tumour (frontal bone osteomyelitis); URGENT
Black or dark discolouration inside nose, on palate, or periorbital skin — invasive fungal sinusitis (mucormycosis) — EMERGENCY; particularly in diabetic or immunocompromised patients

medical_history: Duration of symptoms — <10 days (viral); >10 days without improvement (ABRS criterion); >12 weeks (CRS)
Symptom pattern — which of the 4 cardinal symptoms are present; severity of each (VAS 0-10)
Double worsening pattern — initial improvement then worsening (most specific ABRS criterion)
Unilateral vs bilateral symptoms — unilateral suggests bacterial (ABRS or odontogenic); bilateral suggests viral or allergic
Smell disturbance — sudden onset vs gradual; absent in viral typically (congestion blocks smell transiently); profound chronic anosmia = CRSwNP
Previous episodes — how many; how often; response to antibiotics; any culture results; previous FESS
Allergy history — seasonal or perennial symptoms; hay fever; eczema; asthma; allergen testing previous results; family history of atopy
Asthma — concurrent asthma and sinusitis suggests CRSwNP or AERD; spirometry results
Aspirin sensitivity — does aspirin/ibuprofen trigger facial swelling, nasal polyp exacerbation, or bronchoconstriction? AERD/Samter's triad
Medication history — intranasal sprays already used; antibiotics (which ones; duration); beta-blockers (impair treatment response); ACE inhibitors (nasal congestion side effect); aspirin and NSAIDs
Dental history — upper molar/premolar root canal; dental abscess; recent extraction; implants (odontogenic sinusitis suspicion for unilateral maxillary disease)
Diabetes — uncontrolled diabetes + sinusitis in a diabetic + black tissue = MUCORMYCOSIS until proven otherwise
Immunosuppression — HIV; chemotherapy; transplantation; steroids; haematological malignancy
Occupation — woodworking (adenocarcinoma risk from wood dust — investigate unilateral polyp); hairdressing; chemical exposure; farming
Air pollution exposure — city of residence; proximity to major roads; indoor cooking with biomass fuel
Swimming — competitive swimmer with recurrent sinusitis (P. aeruginosa; water-borne organisms)
COVID-19 history — COVID-19 + steroid treatment + diabetes = mucormycosis risk
physical_examination: General appearance — toxic appearance (high fever, extreme malaise) suggests bacterial or invasive fungal; pallor
Vital signs — temperature; heart rate (tachycardia in severe bacterial or fungal); blood pressure

INSPECTION: facial asymmetry (unilateral swelling suggests dental or tumour); periorbital oedema or erythema; proptosis (bulging eye — orbital complication); frontal swelling (Pott's puffy tumour); black/dark tissue in nasal cavity or palate (invasive fungal — EMERGENCY)

PALPATION: tenderness over maxillary sinuses (below orbital rims — cheekbones); frontal sinus tenderness (above the eyebrows); ethmoid tenderness (medial canthal area — corner of eye); percussion of upper teeth (dental tenderness in odontogenic sinusitis)
TRANSILLUMINATION: shining bright torch against sinus wall in darkened room; opacification vs translucency — limited diagnostic value but simple

Anterior rhinoscopy (with nasal speculum and pen torch): nasal mucosa colour (pale and boggy = allergic; red and inflamed = infectious); nasal discharge character (clear, purulent, bloody); nasal polyps (pale, smooth, translucent, grape-like masses — typically arising from middle meatus); deviated nasal septum; nasal foreign body (especially in children with unilateral foul-smelling discharge); crusting or necrotic tissue

Nasal endoscopy (nasendoscopy — rigid or flexible): by ENT surgeon; gold standard for examining middle meatus, sinus drainage pathways, polyps, tumours; takes biopsies if needed; cultures from middle meatus
Oral examination: upper dental health; upper molar percussion (dental pathology); palate inspection (black necrosis in mucormycosis may appear on palate)
Eye examination: visual acuity; extra-ocular movements; pupillary reflexes; proptosis measurement; chemosis (conjunctival oedema)
Neurological examination: cranial nerve assessment (III, IV, V, VI affected in cavernous sinus thrombosis); neck stiffness (meningism); level of consciousness
Cervical lymphadenopathy — reactive to upper respiratory infection; suppuration from severe ABRS

diagnostic_tests.test_name: CT Scan of Paranasal Sinuses (Coronal Views) — Gold Standard Imaging
diagnostic_tests.description: The definitive imaging modality for evaluating the paranasal sinuses — providing detailed anatomical assessment of all four sinus groups, the osteomeatal complex (the key drainage pathway), nasal anatomy, and orbital and intracranial boundaries. CORONAL VIEWS are most informative for the osteomeatal complex; axial and sagittal reconstructions provide additional information. CT findings in sinusitis: mucosal thickening (>3-4 mm — normal sinus has no visible mucosa on CT); air-fluid levels (indicates active infection with purulent secretion); sinus opacification (complete filling — severe sinusitis); ostial obstruction; bone erosion (concerning for tumour or invasive fungal sinusitis); orbital extension; intracranial extension.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Evaluate extent of CRS and guide surgical planning (pre-FESS); detect complications (orbital, intracranial); diagnose odontogenic sinusitis (dental pathology visible); assess fungal sinusitis (hyperdense fungal ball or expansile soft tissue with bone erosion); staging for FESS; not routinely indicated for uncomplicated acute sinusitis
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Lund-Mackay CT score (0-24): each sinus scored 0-2 (0=clear; 1=partial opacification; 2=complete opacification) for 10 sites bilaterally; total score ≥4 = clinical significance; used for CRS severity stratification; pre- and post-treatment comparison
diagnostic_tests.when_not_to_scan: Routine CT is NOT required for straightforward acute sinusitis (clinical diagnosis + appropriate treatment); CT for: suspected complications; pre-FESS planning; recurrent unexplained sinusitis; CRS not responding to treatment; unilateral disease (exclude tumour); suspected odontogenic cause; immunocompromised with sinusitis
diagnostic_tests.india_note: CT sinuses available at all urban radiology centres in India; cost approximately Rs 2,000-5,000; request specifically 'CT paranasal sinuses with coronal and axial views' — not just 'CT head'

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Nasal Endoscopy (Nasendoscopy) — Gold Standard ENT Examination
diagnostic_tests.description: Rigid or flexible endoscope (2.7 mm or 4 mm diameter) passed through the nasal cavity by an ENT surgeon — providing direct visualisation of the nasal cavity, middle meatus, sinus drainage pathways, posterior choana, and nasopharynx. Essential for CRS diagnosis (objective evidence of mucopus from middle meatus), nasal polyp assessment, tissue biopsy, middle meatal cultures, and post-FESS follow-up.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Objective diagnosis of CRS (mucopus from middle meatus; mucosal inflammation; polyps); assess polyp size and grade; middle meatal culture for ABRS or CRS (targeted antibiotic therapy); biopsy suspicious lesions; post-operative evaluation
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Lund-Kennedy endoscopy score (0-12): polyps (0-2 each side); oedema (0-2); discharge (0-2); scarring (0-2); crusting (0-2); total guides disease severity and treatment monitoring

diagnostic_tests.test_name: MRI of Brain and Paranasal Sinuses (With Contrast)
diagnostic_tests.description: MRI is superior to CT for soft tissue characterisation and evaluating intracranial complications of sinusitis — including meningitis, cerebral abscess, subdural empyema, and cavernous sinus thrombosis. Contrast-enhanced MRI shows: dural enhancement (meningeal irritation); brain abscess ring enhancement; cavernous sinus thrombosis (filling defect); orbital cellulitis vs abscess (subperiosteal abscess shows ring-enhancing collection). MRI also better characterises sinonasal tumours from inflammatory disease. MANDATORY for any suspected intracranial complication.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Intracranial complication assessment (meningitis, abscess, empyema, cavernous sinus thrombosis); distinguish invasive fungal sinusitis from tumour; characterise sinonasal tumours; orbital complication evaluation (subperiosteal abscess)
diagnostic_tests.note: Request 'MRI brain and paranasal sinuses with gadolinium contrast' for suspected complications; faster and more available than MRI — CT used in emergency settings

diagnostic_tests.description: Culture of nasal secretions to identify bacterial pathogens and guide antibiotic therapy. SITE MATTERS — anterior nasal swab (from the nostril) reflects nasal flora and is unreliable for sinus organisms; MIDDLE MEATAL SWAB (obtained under endoscopic guidance from the middle meatus — the sinus drainage pathway) is diagnostically reliable. Sensitivity of middle meatal culture correlates highly (87%) with maxillary sinus aspirate culture (the gold standard). Maxillary sinus puncture and aspiration is occasionally performed for refractory ABRS or suspected complications when culture-directed therapy is essential.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify causative bacteria in ABRS failing first-line antibiotics; detect MRSA or resistant organisms; culture-directed therapy in refractory CRS; pre-operative microbiological assessment in severe CRS
diagnostic_tests.when_to_culture: ABRS not responding to first-line antibiotics; severe or complicated sinusitis; immunocompromised patients; hospital-acquired sinusitis (ventilator-associated); post-surgical sinusitis
diagnostic_tests.india_resistance_note: H. influenzae beta-lactamase production is common in India (40-60%) — justifying co-amoxiclav as first-line over plain amoxicillin; MRSA sinusitis increasing; Pseudomonas relevant in swimmers and immunocompromised

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Allergy Testing — Skin Prick Test (SPT) and Specific IgE (RAST)
diagnostic_tests.description: Identifies specific IgE sensitisation to aeroallergens — essential for patients with allergic rhinosinusitis and CRS. SKIN PRICK TEST: small pricks on forearm with standardised allergen extracts; wheal and flare response at 15-20 minutes indicates IgE sensitisation; highly sensitive; requires stopping antihistamines 5-7 days before; SPECIFIC IgE (ImmunoCAP/RAST): blood test measuring IgE antibody levels to specific allergens; can be performed on antihistamines; useful when SPT not feasible (dermatographism, severe eczema). Key allergens to test in India: house dust mites (D. pteronyssinus, D. farinae — most important in tropical India); cockroach (Blatella germanica); Aspergillus fumigatus; Alternaria alternata (moulds); grass pollens; tree pollens; cat and dog dander.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm allergic rhinosinusitis aetiology; identify specific allergens for avoidance and immunotherapy; guide allergen immunotherapy selection; assess AFRS (elevated total IgE and specific mould IgE)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Wheal ≥3 mm larger than negative control = positive SPT; Specific IgE: Class 0 (<0.35 kU/L) = negative; Class 1+ (>0.35) = sensitised; Class 4+ (>17.5) = high sensitisation
diagnostic_tests.india_note: SPT widely available at allergy clinics in major Indian cities (AIIMS, PGI, Medanta, Apollo, Fortis); important for identifying dust mite sensitisation (very common in India) — enables targeted immunotherapy

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Full Blood Count (FBC) and Inflammatory Markers (CRP, ESR)
diagnostic_tests.description: FBC assesses: EOSINOPHILIA (blood eosinophils >400/mcL — supports eosinophilic CRSwNP, AERD, or AFRS; guides steroid and biologic therapy); NEUTROPHILIA (bacterial infection or fungal in immunocompromised); NEUTROPENIA (increased risk of invasive fungal sinusitis). CRP and ESR: elevated in ABRS and complicated sinusitis; very elevated in orbital or intracranial complications.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess inflammation severity; detect eosinophilia (CRSwNP endotyping for biologic therapy); evaluate immune status; orbital/intracranial complication monitoring
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Eosinophils >400/mcL = eosinophilic phenotype (CRSwNP likely); CRP >100 mg/L in sinusitis = severe infection or complication

diagnostic_tests.description: Total serum IgE: markedly elevated in AFRS (Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis) — typically >1000 IU/mL; moderately elevated in allergic rhinitis and CRSwNP; specific IgE to moulds (Aspergillus, Bipolaris, Alternaria, Curvularia) confirms allergic sensitisation in AFRS.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose AFRS; assess allergic status; guide omalizumab (anti-IgE) eligibility (requires total IgE within specific range for dosing)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Microbiological Culture and KOH Preparation — Invasive Fungal Sinusitis
diagnostic_tests.description: When invasive fungal sinusitis is suspected: tissue biopsy and fluid from the sinus (obtained endoscopically or at surgery) must be sent for: KOH (potassium hydroxide) preparation — rapid examination under microscopy for fungal hyphae (Mucorales show broad, non-septate, ribbon-like hyphae; Aspergillus shows narrow, septate hyphae — morphological distinction has major therapeutic implications); Fungal culture (Sabouraud dextrose agar) — identifies species; speciation guides antifungal selection; Histopathology with PAS (Periodic Acid-Schiff) and Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) staining — gold standard for confirming tissue invasion.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm invasive fungal sinusitis; identify fungal species (Mucorales vs Aspergillus — critical, as they have different treatments); guide antifungal therapy
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Broad non-septate hyphae with right-angle branching = Mucorales (mucormycosis — treat with amphotericin B); narrow septate hyphae with 45° branching = Aspergillus; angioinvasion on histology = invasive disease confirmed
diagnostic_tests.urgency: EMERGENCY processing required — invasive fungal sinusitis progresses in hours to days; call laboratory to expedite KOH results

diagnostic_tests.description: MANDATORY in any patient with invasive fungal sinusitis or mucormycosis — uncontrolled diabetes (particularly DKA) is the dominant risk factor; acidosis promotes Mucorales growth; hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil killing. Also important: identify undiagnosed diabetes in patients with recurrent or chronic sinusitis (immune dysfunction from diabetes worsens sinusitis outcomes).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify DKA (life-threatening; treat concurrently with mucormycosis); screen for undiagnosed diabetes in any patient with invasive fungal sinusitis; optimise glycaemic control during treatment
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Glucose >11 mmol/L + symptoms = diabetes; pH <7.3 + ketones = DKA; HbA1c reflects 3-month average glycaemia

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Cystic Fibrosis Sweat Test and CFTR Mutation Analysis
diagnostic_tests.description: Consider in young patients with bilateral nasal polyps, CRS, recurrent sinusitis, and bronchiectasis — particularly children. CF causes universal CRSwNP from dysfunctional chloride channels impairing mucociliary clearance. Sweat chloride >60 mmol/L = CF diagnosis. CFTR mutation analysis confirms diagnosis. A child presenting with nasal polyps should always have CF excluded.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude cystic fibrosis in young patients with CRSwNP and recurrent pulmonary infections

medicines.note: Sinusitis treatment is fundamentally stratified by aetiology and chronicity. ACUTE VIRAL RHINOSINUSITIS: symptom-only management — no antibiotics; ACUTE BACTERIAL RHINOSINUSITIS: targeted antibiotics (co-amoxiclav) plus INCS; CHRONIC RHINOSINUSITIS: intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) are the cornerstone — the most evidence-based pharmacological treatment for CRS; saline irrigation; allergen management. The widespread inappropriate antibiotic prescribing for sinusitis in India is a major driver of antimicrobial resistance — education that most sinusitis is viral and self-limiting is essential. Nasal saline irrigation is one of the most evidence-based, safe, and inexpensive treatments available for all forms of rhinosinusitis — it should be the first treatment prescribed for every patient.
treatment_principles: 1. MOST SINUSITIS IS VIRAL AND SELF-LIMITING — resist the urge to prescribe antibiotics for every case of sinusitis; reserve antibiotics for documented ABRS (meeting strict clinical criteria)

2. INTRANASAL CORTICOSTEROIDS (INCS) are the backbone of CRS treatment — NOT systemic antibiotics; INCS reduce mucosal inflammation, improve drainage, and reduce polyp size; must be used consistently for ≥3 months to assess benefit

3. NASAL SALINE IRRIGATION is the most evidence-based, safe, and affordable adjunct treatment for all rhinosinusitis — it mechanically clears mucus and crusts, improves mucociliary function, and reduces mucosal oedema; prescribe this first for every rhinosinusitis patient
4. TOPICAL DECONGESTANTS (oxymetazoline, xylometazoline) maximum 3-5 days — rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) develops with prolonged use
5. ANTIBIOTICS FOR ABRS: co-amoxiclav (amoxicillin-clavulanate) is first-line in India; duration 5-7 days; NOT 14-21 days (no evidence supports longer duration and increases resistance/side effects)
6. INVASIVE FUNGAL SINUSITIS: EMERGENCY — IV liposomal amphotericin B + emergency surgical debridement; no delay

categories.category_name: Nasal Saline Irrigation — Most Evidence-Based Treatment for All Rhinosinusitis
categories.purpose: Mechanical lavage of the nasal cavity and sinuses to clear mucus, crust, allergens, pollutants, and inflammatory debris; improve mucociliary clearance; reduce mucosal oedema; wash out inflammatory mediators; support healthy nasal microbiome.

medicines.name: Isotonic Saline Nasal Irrigation (Jal Neti / Nasal Douche / Neti Pot)
medicines.form: Nasal rinse sachets dissolved in distilled or boiled cooled water; neti pot; squeeze bottle; powered irrigator
medicines.preparation: Mix 1 sachet (sodium chloride + sodium bicarbonate) in 240 mL of BOILED AND COOLED or DISTILLED WATER (NEVER tap water directly in India — risk of Naegleria fowleri and other waterborne pathogens in nasal cavity); tilt head laterally; pour into upper nostril; fluid exits lower nostril; sniff gently but do not force water into Eustachian tube
medicines.dosage: Twice daily (morning and evening) for active sinusitis; once daily for maintenance prevention; use warm water (37°C) for comfort
medicines.evidence: Cochrane systematic review: nasal saline irrigation reduces symptoms, reduces antibiotic use, and improves quality of life in both acute and chronic sinusitis; Grade A evidence; the WHO recommends saline irrigation for all rhinosinusitis
medicines.india_traditional_note: Jal neti — nasal water cleansing with a neti pot — is a traditional yogic practice (Shatkarma) used in India for thousands of years; well-aligned with modern evidence; widely available neti pots at Rs 100-200; traditional practice validated by modern evidence
medicines.hypertonic_saline: Hypertonic saline (2-3% NaCl) has slightly greater anti-oedema effect vs isotonic (0.9%) — greater osmotic gradient draws fluid from swollen mucosa; some patients find it more irritating; use isotonic for regular maintenance; hypertonic for acute flares

medicines.name: Isotonic Saline Nasal Spray — Aqueous
medicines.dosage: 2-4 sprays each nostril two to four times daily
medicines.use_case: Maintenance moisture and mucociliary support; less washing effect than irrigation but more convenient; for mild symptoms or infants (gentle spray); use throughout the day between irrigations

categories.category_name: Intranasal Corticosteroids (INCS) — Cornerstone of CRS Treatment
categories.purpose: Reduce sinonasal mucosal inflammation; shrink nasal polyps; improve ostial patency allowing sinus drainage; improve olfaction; reduce symptom burden. First-line and most evidence-based pharmacological treatment for chronic rhinosinusitis (both with and without polyps). Minimal systemic absorption — safe for long-term use.

medicines.name: Mometasone Furoate Nasal Spray
medicines.form: Aqueous nasal spray (50 mcg per actuation)
medicines.dosage: CRS/CRSwNP: 2 sprays each nostril twice daily (200 mcg/day); Maintenance after FESS: 2 sprays each nostril once daily; Children ≥6 years: 1-2 sprays once daily
medicines.use_case: The most widely prescribed INCS for CRS; approved for nasal polyps; very low systemic bioavailability (<1%) — safe for long-term use; reduces nasal polyp size (clinical trials show measurable reduction over 4-12 months); recommended first-line in EPOS 2020 and ISG guidelines
medicines.technique: IMPORTANT: correct spray technique essential for efficacy: shake bottle; tilt head slightly forward (NOT back — this sends spray to throat); aim spray toward the outer corner of the eye (NOT toward the nasal septum — septum contact causes epistaxis); sniff GENTLY after spraying; blow nose before spraying to clear mucus; spray AFTER saline irrigation (clears secretions first, allowing INCS to contact mucosa)
side_effects: Mild: nasal dryness; crusting; epistaxis (1-3% — reduced by correct lateral spray angle technique)
Rare: nasal septal perforation (with prolonged incorrect spraying directly onto septum)
Systemic effects minimal (<1% bioavailability) — appropriate at therapeutic doses even in children; bone density effect not clinically significant at standard doses
medicines.duration: Minimum 3 months to assess efficacy for CRS; long-term maintenance (years) required for polyp control; do not stop abruptly in CRSwNP — polyps recur rapidly

medicines.name: Fluticasone Propionate or Furoate Nasal Spray
medicines.form: Aqueous spray (50 mcg and 27.5 mcg per actuation for furoate)
medicines.dosage: Fluticasone propionate: 2 sprays each nostril once daily; Fluticasone furoate: 2 sprays each nostril once daily
medicines.use_case: Excellent INCS option; fluticasone furoate (Veramyst/Avamys) has lowest systemic bioavailability of any INCS (<0.5%) — preferred in children, adrenal-suppression-concerned patients; strong evidence for allergic rhinosinusitis

medicines.name: Budesonide Nasal Spray / Nasal Drops
medicines.dosage: Spray: 2 sprays each nostril once daily; High-volume drops for CRSwNP: 128 mcg (2 drops) each nostril twice daily in 'head down and forward' (HDF) position
medicines.use_case: Particularly useful for CRSwNP — high-volume budesonide nasal drops in HDF position deliver medication into the ethmoid sinuses (where polyps arise); superior polyp penetration compared to sprays; commonly used post-FESS; also used for AFRS
medicines.hdf_technique: Kneel on the floor; bend head forward and downward (head upside-down); instil drops; remain in this position for 5 minutes; the gravity-dependent position directs drops toward the ethmoid roof

medicines.name: Beclomethasone Dipropionate Nasal Spray
medicines.dosage: 2 sprays each nostril twice daily
medicines.use_case: Well-established, affordable INCS; widely available in India; good efficacy for allergic rhinosinusitis; slightly higher systemic bioavailability than mometasone or fluticasone — mometasone/fluticasone preferred for long-term use especially in children

categories.category_name: Antibiotics — ABRS Only (Not Routine for All Sinusitis)
categories.purpose: Targeted bacterial coverage for documented acute bacterial rhinosinusitis meeting clinical criteria — NOT empirical treatment for all sinusitis. First-line: amoxicillin-clavulanate (co-amoxiclav) in India to cover H. influenzae beta-lactamase producing strains.

medicines.name: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (Co-Amoxiclav) — First-Line Antibiotic for ABRS in India
medicines.form: Tablet (625 mg = 500 mg amoxicillin + 125 mg clavulanate; 1g = 875 mg + 125 mg)
medicines.dosage: Adults: 625 mg (500/125) three times daily × 5-7 days; OR 1g (875/125) twice daily × 5-7 days (better compliance); Children: 45 mg/kg/day amoxicillin component in 2-3 divided doses × 5-7 days
medicines.use_case: First-line antibiotic for ABRS in India: covers S. pneumoniae; H. influenzae including beta-lactamase producing strains (clavulanate inhibits beta-lactamase); Moraxella catarrhalis (both beta-lactamase producing and not); most appropriate antibiotic given India's resistance patterns
medicines.mechanism: Amoxicillin: broad-spectrum aminopenicillin — inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis; Clavulanate: beta-lactamase inhibitor — prevents amoxicillin inactivation by bacterial enzymes
side_effects: Diarrhoea (10-15% — GI intolerance from clavulanate; take WITH FOOD to reduce)
Amoxicillin rash (5% of patients — more common if EBV mononucleosis — widespread rash is not true penicillin allergy)
medicines.duration: 5-7 days is sufficient for ABRS — studies show no benefit of 10-14 day courses; shorter courses reduce adverse effects and resistance selection
medicines.failure: If no improvement after 72 hours on co-amoxiclav — reassess diagnosis; consider middle meatal culture; switch to respiratory fluoroquinolone or moxifloxacin
medicines.india_note: Plain amoxicillin (without clavulanate) is INSUFFICIENT for ABRS in India — H. influenzae beta-lactamase production in India is ~40-60%; always use co-amoxiclav

medicines.name: Levofloxacin or Moxifloxacin — Respiratory Fluoroquinolones (Second-Line ABRS)
medicines.dosage: Levofloxacin 500 mg once daily × 5-7 days; Moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily × 5 days
medicines.use_case: Second-line for ABRS failing co-amoxiclav; penicillin allergy (true allergy — anaphylaxis, not rash); MRSA risk (moxifloxacin has good MRSA coverage); very effective against S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, atypicals
medicines.note: Reserve fluoroquinolones as second-line — broad spectrum drives resistance to quinolones in India (already high rates); avoid as routine first-line therapy for sinusitis

medicines.name: Azithromycin or Clarithromycin — Macrolides (Third-Line / Atypical Cover)
medicines.dosage: Azithromycin 500 mg once daily × 3-5 days; Clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily × 5-7 days
medicines.use_case: Third-line ABRS — macrolide resistance among S. pneumoniae in India is very high (>30-40%); use only if co-amoxiclav and fluoroquinolones are contraindicated; azithromycin has additional anti-inflammatory properties (benefits chronic inflammation — used at low dose for CRSsNP in some protocols)
medicines.long_dose_azithromycin_crs: Low-dose azithromycin 250 mg three times per week for 3 months — has anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects on sinonasal mucosa (inhibits IL-8, reduces biofilm formation); used in some CRSsNP protocols as adjunct — not first-line; BEFORE using long-term azithromycin: check NTM status (non-tuberculous mycobacteria — azithromycin monotherapy promotes NTM resistance); baseline ECG (QT interval)

medicines.name: Cefuroxime Axetil (Oral Cephalosporin) — Penicillin-Allergic Patients (Non-Anaphylaxis)
medicines.dosage: 500 mg twice daily × 5-7 days
medicines.use_case: Alternative for mild penicillin allergy (rash — not anaphylaxis); covers S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae; ~10-15% cross-reactivity with penicillin — use with caution in true anaphylaxis history

categories.category_name: Topical Decongestants — Short-Term Symptom Relief Only
categories.purpose: Rapid reduction of nasal mucosal vasodilatation and oedema — providing almost immediate nasal decongestion; facilitates sinus ostial drainage; allows INCS to penetrate further into sinonasal cavity (use decongestant 15-20 minutes before INCS in acute phase); CRITICAL LIMITATION: maximum 3-5 days use — prolonged use causes RHINITIS MEDICAMENTOSA (rebound congestion — the nasal mucosa becomes progressively more congested requiring more decongestant, creating dependency).

medicines.name: Oxymetazoline Hydrochloride Nasal Spray — 0.05%
medicines.dosage: 2-3 sprays each nostril twice daily (morning and night); STRICTLY MAXIMUM 3-5 DAYS; Children 6-12 years: Nasivion 0.025% — 2 drops/sprays each nostril twice daily; Children 2-5 years: 0.01% formula; Infants under 2 years: paediatric formulation only under medical guidance
medicines.mechanism: Alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist — causes vasoconstriction of nasal mucosal blood vessels; reduces mucosal oedema within 2-3 minutes; duration of action 10-12 hours (oxymetazoline); 8-10 hours (xylometazoline)
medicines.rhinitis_medicamentosa: REBOUND CONGESTION — after more than 5 days of use, the nasal mucosa becomes hypersensitive and increasingly congested as each dose wears off, requiring more frequent use; leads to chronic nasal obstruction that is difficult to treat; managed by: gradual withdrawal; ipratropium nasal spray as bridge; INCS initiated concurrently; weaning over 4-6 weeks
medicines.contraindications: Narrow-angle glaucoma; severe hypertension; thyrotoxicosis; concurrent MAOI use (hypertensive crisis); avoid in children <2 years without medical supervision

medicines.name: Pseudoephedrine (Oral Decongestant)
brand_examples: Combination cold medicines containing pseudoephedrine: various brands
medicines.dosage: 60 mg every 4-6 hours; maximum 240 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Systemic decongestant; longer duration than topical; less risk of rebound congestion; useful when topical spray not appropriate; commonly combined with antihistamines in 'cold and sinusitis tablets'
medicines.side_effects: Insomnia; palpitations; tachycardia; hypertension; urinary retention in BPH
medicines.india_note: Schedule H drug in India — requires prescription; contained in many OTC combination cold preparations (check for pseudoephedrine content); misuse potential as methamphetamine precursor (regulatory restrictions)

categories.purpose: Block H1 histamine receptors — reducing histamine-mediated allergic symptoms (sneezing, itching, watery discharge); second-generation (non-sedating) antihistamines preferred; most effective for the allergic rhinitis component of rhinosinusitis.

medicines.name: Cetirizine Hydrochloride — Second-Generation (Non-Sedating)
medicines.dosage: Adults: 10 mg once daily at night (mild sedation possible — take at bedtime); Children 6-12 years: 5 mg twice daily or 10 mg once daily; 2-6 years: 2.5 mg twice daily
medicines.use_case: Allergic rhinosinusitis (sneezing, itching, watery rhinorrhoea); adjunct to INCS for CRS with allergic component; widely affordable and available in India
medicines.mechanism: Selective H1 receptor inverse agonist; minimal CNS penetration (minor sedation only); also has anti-inflammatory properties (reduces eosinophil migration)
medicines.note: Most effective for sneezing and itching of allergic rhinitis; less effective for nasal congestion (INCS superior for congestion)

medicines.name: Fexofenadine Hydrochloride — Truly Non-Sedating
medicines.dosage: 180 mg once daily (adults); 120 mg twice daily for children
medicines.use_case: Preferred when no sedation tolerated (drivers, pilots, operators of heavy machinery); allergic rhinosinusitis; excellent safety profile; does not cross blood-brain barrier

medicines.name: Loratadine
medicines.dosage: 10 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Allergic rhinosinusitis; non-sedating; widely available; safe in pregnancy (Category B)

medicines.name: Levocetirizine — More Potent Isomer
medicines.dosage: 5 mg once daily at night
medicines.use_case: Chronic allergic rhinosinusitis; slightly more potent than cetirizine; mild sedation; good for night-time dosing

categories.category_name: Systemic Corticosteroids — Short Course for CRSwNP and Severe Allergic Rhinosinusitis
categories.purpose: Rapidly reduce severe sinonasal eosinophilic inflammation and nasal polyp volume — used as short-course 'medical polypectomy' in severe CRSwNP before FESS or when surgery is contraindicated.

medicines.name: Prednisolone (Oral) — Short Course
medicines.dosage: CRSwNP 'medical polypectomy': 30-40 mg once daily × 5-7 days (fixed short course); OR tapering: 50 mg → 40 mg → 30 mg → 20 mg → 10 mg × 2 days each (10-day course); DO NOT use prolonged courses due to systemic side effects; Severe allergic rhinosinusitis exacerbation: 20-30 mg × 5 days
medicines.use_case: Severe CRSwNP causing complete obstruction or severe anosmia; pre-FESS preparation; post-FESS eosinophilic exacerbation; acute exacerbation of AERD
medicines.mechanism: Broad anti-inflammatory; suppresses eosinophilic Th2 inflammation; reduces polyp oedema and size; restores smell dramatically (often anosmia improves within 24-48 hours of steroid — the 'steroid sniff test' used diagnostically)
medicines.the_steroid_sniff_test: If anosmia improves significantly with a 5-7 day prednisolone course, this confirms CRSwNP anosmia is conductive (mechanical obstruction) and potentially reversible — suggests surgery will restore smell
medicines.side_effects: Short course (<10 days): fluid retention; mood changes; insomnia; blood glucose elevation (particularly important in diabetics); adrenal suppression minimal
medicines.contraindications: Uncontrolled diabetes (relative — monitor glucose closely); active infection; glaucoma

medicines.name: Dexamethasone (Oral or IV) — Severe Sinonasal Emergencies
medicines.dosage: IV 4-8 mg every 6-8 hours (severe orbital cellulitis adjunct)
medicines.use_case: Adjunct to antibiotics for severe orbital cellulitis; NOT for routine sinusitis

categories.category_name: Leukotriene Receptor Antagonists — CRS with Polyps and AERD

medicines.name: Montelukast
medicines.form: Tablet (10 mg adult; 5 mg chewable for children 6-14 years; 4 mg granules for 2-6 years)
medicines.dosage: Adults: 10 mg once daily at night; Children 6-14 years: 5 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Adjunct treatment for CRSwNP (reduces polyp recurrence post-FESS); AERD (blocks cysteinyl leukotriene pathway — helps prevent NSAID-triggered exacerbations of nasal polyps and asthma); concurrent allergic rhinitis and mild asthma (both indications); useful when INCS alone insufficient
medicines.mechanism: Selective CysLT1 receptor antagonist — blocks leukotriene-mediated eosinophilic inflammation; particularly relevant in AERD where aspirin shifts arachidonic acid metabolism toward leukotrienes
medicines.side_effects: Generally well-tolerated; neuropsychiatric adverse effects (FDA black box warning 2020): depression, suicidal ideation, nightmares, agitation — particularly in children and adolescents; assess baseline mental health; discuss risks with patients/parents; discontinue if neuropsychiatric symptoms develop
medicines.india_note: FDA neuropsychiatric warning (2020) has not been as widely communicated in India; important to counsel patients; particularly cautious use in adolescents with pre-existing depression

categories.purpose: Targeted monoclonal antibodies blocking specific cytokines in the Th2 eosinophilic inflammatory cascade driving severe CRSwNP — revolutionising treatment of patients with uncontrolled disease despite INCS and repeated surgeries.

medicines.name: Dupilumab (Anti-IL-4Rα) — The Most Effective Biologic for CRSwNP
medicines.form: Subcutaneous injection (300 mg/2 mL pre-filled syringe)
medicines.dosage: 300 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks (self-administered pre-filled syringe); Loading dose: 600 mg × 1 then 300 mg every 2 weeks
medicines.use_case: Severe uncontrolled CRSwNP — indicated when: bilateral nasal polyps with significant symptoms (TPS ≥5) despite intranasal corticosteroids AND has had or is a candidate for FESS; concurrent asthma significantly benefits; dramatically reduces polyp size, improves smell, reduces nasal congestion, reduces need for oral steroids and repeat surgery
medicines.mechanism: Fully human monoclonal antibody blocking IL-4Rα — the shared receptor subunit for IL-4 and IL-13 (the key Th2 cytokines driving eosinophilic inflammation); blocks both IL-4 and IL-13 signalling simultaneously — the most upstream and complete Th2 blockade available; reduces nasal polyp burden by ~40% reduction in nasal polyp score at 24 weeks
medicines.evidence: SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials: dupilumab significantly reduced nasal polyp score, improved SNOT-22 quality of life, improved loss of smell, reduced nasal congestion, and dramatically reduced need for oral steroids and sinus surgery vs placebo; approved by FDA (2019) and EMA for severe CRSwNP
medicines.cost_india: Currently very expensive in India — approximately Rs 50,000-70,000 per injection (bimonthly injections = approximately Rs 1,200,000-1,680,000 annually); not yet available on government insurance; Roche compassionate use programme for selected patients; biosimilar expected to reduce costs substantially
medicines.side_effects: Generally well-tolerated; injection site reactions; conjunctivitis (occurs in 10-20% of CRSwNP patients — possibly from reduced IL-13 in goblet cells causing dry eye); arthralgia

medicines.name: Mepolizumab (Anti-IL-5) — Severe CRSwNP with Eosinophilic Asthma
medicines.dosage: 100 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks (monthly)
medicines.use_case: Severe eosinophilic CRSwNP with concurrent severe eosinophilic asthma; approved for both indications; reduces polyp size and asthma exacerbations
medicines.mechanism: Anti-IL-5 monoclonal antibody — reduces eosinophil production, survival, and activation

medicines.name: Omalizumab (Anti-IgE) — CRSwNP with Allergic Component and Asthma
medicines.dosage: 150-600 mg subcutaneously every 2-4 weeks (dose based on baseline total IgE and body weight)
medicines.use_case: CRSwNP with concurrent allergic rhinitis and asthma; also approved for AFRS; reduces total IgE and IgE-mediated inflammation; reduces polyp burden and improves asthma control

categories.purpose: Targeted antifungal therapy for invasive fungal sinusitis — a medical emergency; treatment delay significantly worsens outcome.

medicines.name: Liposomal Amphotericin B — First-Line for Mucormycosis (Invasive Fungal Sinusitis)
medicines.dosage: Mucormycosis: 5-10 mg/kg/day IV; duration: 4-6 weeks minimum (guided by clinical response and imaging); step down to isavuconazole or posaconazole when stable
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE treatment for ALL invasive mucormycosis (rhinosinusitis, rhino-orbital, rhinocerebral); liposomal formulation preferred over conventional amphotericin B — significantly less nephrotoxic while maintaining equivalent antifungal efficacy; also effective against Aspergillus
medicines.mechanism: Polyene antifungal — binds ergosterol in fungal cell membrane creating pores causing cell leakage and death; liposomal encapsulation preferentially accumulates in infected tissue reducing renal toxicity
medicines.monitoring: Renal function (creatinine, electrolytes) daily — nephrotoxicity; magnesium and potassium replacement (renal wasting); infusion-related reactions (rigors, fever — premedicate with paracetamol and antihistamine); LFTs
medicines.india_covid_note: Liposomal amphotericin B was in critical shortage during the COVID-19-associated mucormycosis epidemic in 2021 in India; government requisitioned global supplies; this shortage was a major contributor to treatment delays and mortality

medicines.name: Isavuconazole — Step-Down Oral Therapy for Mucormycosis
medicines.dosage: Loading: isavuconazonium sulphate 372 mg every 8h × 48h (6 doses); Maintenance: 372 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Step-down oral therapy for mucormycosis when patient is stable on IV amphotericin B; also appropriate for Aspergillus; better tolerated and fewer drug interactions than voriconazole for mucormycosis

medicines.name: Voriconazole — First-Line for Aspergillus Invasive Sinusitis
medicines.form: IV infusion; Oral tablet; Oral suspension
medicines.dosage: IV: 6 mg/kg every 12h × 2 doses loading; then 4 mg/kg every 12h maintenance; Oral: 200 mg twice daily (adult >40 kg) — highly bioavailable orally; step down when clinically stable
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE for invasive Aspergillus sinusitis; NOT for Mucorales (voriconazole does not cover Mucorales — this is a critical distinction; using voriconazole for mucormycosis is ineffective and delays correct treatment)
medicines.note: Always determine fungal species before selecting antifungal: Mucorales (broad non-septate hyphae on KOH) → amphotericin B; Aspergillus (narrow septate hyphae) → voriconazole

medicines.name: Itraconazole — Allergic Fungal Rhinosinusitis (AFRS) and Chronic Non-Invasive Fungal Sinusitis
medicines.dosage: 200 mg twice daily for 3-6 months
medicines.use_case: Adjunct to FESS for AFRS (reduces recurrence); NOT appropriate for invasive fungal disease; chronic non-invasive fungal sinusitis

categories.category_name: Allergen Immunotherapy (AIT) — Disease-Modifying Treatment for Allergic Rhinosinusitis
categories.purpose: The only disease-modifying treatment for allergic rhinitis — can achieve long-term symptom reduction persisting after treatment completion; reduces the risk of CRS development and nasal polyp formation; reduces risk of allergic rhinitis progressing to asthma.

medicines.name: Subcutaneous Allergen Immunotherapy (SCIT)
medicines.description: Gradually increasing doses of identified allergen extract injected subcutaneously weekly for 3-5 years; 'trains' the immune system to tolerate allergens by shifting Th2 response to Th1 and inducing regulatory T cells; requires allergy clinic with resuscitation facilities (anaphylaxis risk); highly effective particularly for house dust mite, grass pollen, and cat dander allergy
medicines.dosage: Build-up phase: weekly injections for 4-6 months (increasing concentrations); maintenance phase: monthly injections for 3-5 years
medicines.india_availability: Available at allergy clinics in major Indian cities (AIIMS Delhi, PGI Chandigarh, PGIMER, private allergy centres); relatively affordable (Rs 500-2,000/month); very effective for house dust mite allergy (most common allergen in India)

medicines.name: Sublingual Immunotherapy (SLIT) — Drops or Tablets
medicines.description: Allergen extracts administered under the tongue daily; administered at home (no clinic visits after first prescription); less anaphylaxis risk than SCIT; lower compliance due to daily self-administration; effective for house dust mite and grass pollen allergy; particularly useful for children; SLIT tablets approved for dust mite and grass: ACARIZAX (house dust mite tablet); GRAZAX (grass pollen tablet)
medicines.dosage: Daily sublingual administration; build-up phase: 4-12 weeks; maintenance: 3-5 years
medicines.india_note: SLIT drops widely available in India (multiple brands of polyvalent extracts); convenience of home administration improves compliance vs SCIT; increasingly preferred in Indian allergy practice

medicines.name: Aspirin Desensitisation Protocol
medicines.description: Gradual oral aspirin challenge under medical supervision — starting with very small doses (20.25 mg) and increasing every 3 hours to full therapeutic dose (325-650 mg); once tolerant, daily aspirin therapy maintained; after successful desensitisation, patients can take aspirin and other NSAIDs; reduces nasal polyp recurrence, improves olfaction, reduces asthma exacerbations
